CHIEF COMPLAINT
Nonhealing right foot ulcer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Gregory is a patient with a right foot ulcer that has been present for approximately two months. The ulcer developed after walking barefoot on Dewey Beach. Over the past few weeks, the ulcer has become increasingly concerning with onset of redness and drainage, which prompted him to seek evaluation. He denies severe pain but reports occasional throbbing sensations. His primary concern is the recent development of drainage and redness. His PCP previously prescribed antibiotics; however, the patient has not yet filled the prescription and cannot recall the specific medication name, though he believes he may have taken it previously.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient reports occasional throbbing at the ulcer site without distinct pain. Endorses recent onset of redness and drainage. Denies fever. Reports increased pressure sensation on examination but no severe pain.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Diabetes mellitus. Patient reports taking diabetes medication but does not regularly check blood glucose. Last reported A1C approximately 10.

MEDICATIONS
Diabetes medication (specific agent not specified).

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Works as an ambulance driver. Recent visit to Dewey Beach where patient sustained foot injury from walking barefoot.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs normal, no fever. Right foot examination reveals a 1 x 2 inch circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot, proximal to the fifth metatarsophalangeal joint, with associated redness, drainage, and edema. No necrosis, odor, or bony exposure noted. Palpation elicits increased pressure sensation without distinct pain.

RESULTS
Right foot X-ray: No evidence of osteomyelitis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Diabetic foot ulcer with infection. Ankle Brachial Index ordered to assess blood supply to foot. Wound debridement performed to remove necrotic tissue. Clindamycin 400 mg PO twice daily for 7 days prescribed for infection management. Surgical offloading shoe provided for one month to reduce pressure on ulcer. Follow-up appointment scheduled in 2 weeks for reassessment and possible repeat debridement. Patient instructed to call office with any concerns and to seek urgent care or emergency evaluation if fever, worsening symptoms, or other emergencies develop.
